name: Quantum Magnetometers
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Mapping Fields No Compass Can Find
lesson.summary: Quantum magnetometers use the extreme sensitivity of atomic and solid-state quantum systems to detect magnetic fields thousands of times fainter than Earth's own, and they are already deployed in hospitals, mines, and defense labs.
lesson.body:
Recall from quantum sensing that the core trick is to find a quantum system whose internal state changes in a precise, calculable way when an external field pushes on it, then measure that change with enough precision to back out the field. Magnetic fields are one of the easiest quantities to couple to a quantum system this way, because the energy levels of an atom, or the spin of an electron, shift measurably in the presence of a magnetic field, an effect called the Zeeman effect. A quantum magnetometer is built to make that shift as easy as possible to read out.

Three main technologies do this job today. Superconducting quantum interference devices, or SQUIDs, use loops of superconducting material interrupted by thin insulating junctions. The quantum interference of electron pairs tunneling across those junctions is exquisitely sensitive to magnetic flux, down to tiny fractions of a single flux quantum. Optically pumped magnetometers use a small glass cell of alkali vapor, often rubidium, whose atoms are aligned by laser light and then precess in a magnetic field at a rate set by the field strength, which a second laser beam reads out. Nitrogen vacancy centers in diamond use a single defect, a missing carbon atom next to a nitrogen impurity, whose electron spin state can be initialized and read out optically at room temperature, with no cryogenics required.

These are not lab curiosities. Optically pumped magnetometers are now small enough to sit directly against a person's scalp in a lightweight helmet, which matters because magnetoencephalography, or MEG, measures the tiny magnetic fields produced by electrical activity in the brain. Older MEG systems used SQUIDs that had to be kept near absolute zero inside a bulky helmet fixed at one size, forcing patients to hold their head still inside a room-sized shield. Companies now building OPM-based MEG helmets let the sensors sit flush against the skin and move with the patient, a real improvement for imaging children or anyone who cannot stay still, including people being monitored during epileptic seizures.

Outside medicine, magnetometers are used to search for buried ferrous objects such as unexploded ordnance, to map subsurface mineral and ore bodies for exploration companies, to detect submarines by their disturbance of Earth's magnetic field, and to check welds and aircraft parts for hidden cracks without cutting them open. None of these applications need a quantum computer, or even qubits performing logic. They need one very sensitive quantum probe, reading one physical quantity, over and over, and that distinction turns out to matter a great deal for how close this technology already is to market, a point we will return to shortly.
